title: 130 feet from disaster: What we learned about the deadliest airline crash in decades - NewsBreak
text: Hours of testimony and thousands of pages of documents made public Wednesday by federal accident investigators probing the deadliest U.S. airline crash in decades painted a picture of the airspace in Washington as so busy and complicated that even small mistakes made that day in January resulted in disastrous consequences. The first of what will be a three-day fact-finding hearing into the details of a crash involving a military helicopter and a commercial airliner near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport showcased a brutally unforgiving airspace complicated by overlapping flight routes, different procedures used by a myriad of agencies including the military, overburdened air traffic controllers and razor thin margins for error. “The Washington area is one of the most complex airspace regions in the United States, due to its multiple airports, the restricted airspace surrounding the National Capitol Region, and the high volume of diverse air traffic including commercial, military, law enforcement, and news media helicopters,” an NTSB report made public Wednesday reads. Here are some details revealed Wednesday about what went wrong in the skies near Washington: The Army Black Hawk helicopter’s altimeter wasn’t sensitive enough. Air traffic controllers cleared the helicopter to cross behind the commercial airplane as it was landing, relying on the military pilots to see the plane and avoid it. But preliminary data shows that the helicopter had been flying at about 300 feet above the ground — about 100 feet higher than it should have been — placing it on a collision course with the PSA Airlines passenger airplane as it tried to land. The Black Hawk’s altimeter, an instrument that helps pilots gauge how high above the ground an aircraft is flying, can be inaccurate by up to 130 feet, NTSB investigators found. The Army largely downplayed concerns about the discrepancy, saying it was within the parameters of the helicopter’s capabilities. U.S. Army Chief Warrant Officer Kylene Lewis, testifying on behalf of the branch, said a discrepancy of 100 feet wouldn’t be a “cause for alarm” and would be acceptable for military helicopter operations. The military pilots are believed to have been wearing night-vision goggles, which can make visual cues difficult to identify in bright environments. The helicopter was on a training flight that night, and though NTSB investigators haven’t been able to definitively say they were wearing night vision goggles, the pilots took off intending to use them. The goggles, especially in bright urban environments like Washington, can be difficult to use — and often other aircraft can be hard to distinguish. Shortly before the collision, the helicopter’s pilot said she had the jet in sight, but investigators are probing whether she might have seen a different plane instead. According to one document, a pilot with the U.S. Army Aviation Brigade where the helicopter was based told investigators that “cultural lighting and related dimming” made it difficult to use night vision goggles in the area. The pilot said that aircraft looked like “point sources of light" without a recognizable silhouette, surrounded by “halos,” similar to many lights on the ground. Some PSA Airline pilots were not familiar with the helicopter routes around the airport. Out of four PSA Airline pilots that have flown into Reagan National interviewed for the investigation, only one was aware of helicopter routes around the airport and their boundaries. The others said they “did not know that published helicopter routes existed” despite having landed at the airport previously. One pilot even stated that having that information would have been “really helpful for us to have [had] more awareness if we would've known that there's like a specific helicopter route in that area.” Helicopter routes near the airport are designed in tight layers with little room for error. The helicopter route used by the Black Hawk involved in the crash is designed in stacked layers, where helicopters are supposed to be able to pass well underneath planes, though they are often told to wait until they are clear of commercial traffic. Margins are in the hundreds of feet, meaning even a small drift — as what appears to have happened in January — can result in disaster. The air traffic controller approved the helicopter to approach the airport after the plane had passed in front of it. But according to documents and testimony Wednesday, it was more typical for controllers to ask helicopters not to approach the airport until after the plane had already safely cleared the area. Testifying Wednesday on behalf of the Army, Col. Andy DeForest said it would be customary to wait. If a plane was landing, “we'd be holding” at a geographical marker colloquially called the “golf balls,” DeForest said. “So this was very unusual that this occurred." Separately, Army Chief Warrant Officer David Van Vechten said knowing that the separation between aircraft is so limited, the pilots should have been told “not to cross the center line of the approach path until you saw the [plane] either take off or land.” NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said officials have known the routes in the area need to be modified for many years, citing findings from a safety panel noting that the routes have “changed very little since 1999 while airlines, aircraft types approaches, volume, complexity, crews and many other factors have evolved.” Meanwhile, Homendy recited helicopter operations that trigger “safety events” have been “increasing year over year." Homendy lit into FAA officials for dragging their feet on pursuing changes. “Everybody in FAA, in the tower, was saying there was a problem. But you guys are pointing out, 'Well, our bureaucratic process, somebody should have brought it up at some other symposium.' ... Are you kidding me? 67 people are dead!" she said. A working group of local controllers recommended the helicopter route in use on the day of the crash be eliminated. The effort died after management declared it “too political.” An ad hoc working group that included air traffic controllers at Reagan National previously sought changes to a helicopter route at the center of the crash, known as Route 4. The group surveyed the complicated airspace around Washington and proposed removing the route , but the documents said a manager declared those changes to be “too political” to move forward. Clark Allen, an air traffic control specialist with FAA involved in the working group, confirmed there had been movement to shift the route farther eastward — but it never went anywhere. Helicopter operators have different procedures for navigating the area — with the Army among the least risk-averse. NTSB documents made public Wednesday showed the various agencies that fly helicopters in the region, including the Army, Air Force, Coast Guard, local law enforcement and medical transportation outfits maintain a patchwork of protocols for flying near the airport, with some accepting more risk than others. For instance, Army pilots were trained to fly routes at altitudes published by the FAA, but routinely deviated higher if they were using night vision goggles. Meanwhile, law enforcement typically takes pains to stay lower than the “conflict layer” zone near the airport, where different aircraft can intersect. The Coast Guard deliberately stayed clear of the airport during very busy times, as did the Air Force. A key location transmitting technology on the Black Hawk either was not turned on, or inoperable. A technology known as ADS-B, which broadcasts location, speed and altitude of an aircraft for controllers to see on their displays, was not engaged on the Black Hawk. Military and other security-focused agencies routinely disable it for flights in the region, according to lawmakers that have been critical of the practice. In March, the FAA mandated that nearly all aircraft must have it turned on, with limited exceptions. But Rick Dressler, the aviation site manager for medical services company Metro Aviation, told NTSB investigators he's observed other helicopter operators still not turning on the technology "to this day." It had been an open question about whether the helicopter was purposefully not using the technology, or if it had been inoperable — but on Wednesday, Homendy said actual data hadn't been transmitting from that particular helicopter for months. DeForest, the Army official, on Wednesday said it takes several steps to turn it off on that particular helicopter model, suggesting a trickier process to undo — but that it is not the Army’s policy to switch it off while in-flight.
